The story contains several character and thematic turns that are unexpected yet fit seamlessly into the established narrative. Most notably, the ending subverts the reader's expectation of how the narrator will feel once the miserable, eighteen-month construction ordeal is finally over. Instead of feeling pure relief, the narrator admits to feeling glad they didn't get a job at a dry, new university in Arizona, and even feels "almost disappointed" when the building no longer leaks on a rainy day—going so far as to crack a window to let the dampness in. 

While it is surprising that someone would miss a moldy, deafening, and freezing work environment, the turn is entirely appropriate. The narrator has spent the entire story demonstrating how quickly human beings normalize misery ("the speed with which suffering becomes décor") and how shared hardship creates a "grim membership" and sense of purpose. Furthermore, the narrator's final action—opening the window—appropriately echoes two earlier, smaller turns: Priya's newborn baby sleeping peacefully through the jackhammering because she was conditioned to it in the womb, and the Facilities man's unexpectedly poetic observation that "water has a memory." The narrator, like the baby and the water, has been conditioned by the environment, making the final twist both surprising and deeply coherent.
